title: Font families and fallback stacks
learningObjectives: Explain font families and fallback stacks and apply it in a readable interface.

understand.concept: The font-family property lists preferred typefaces in order. The browser uses the first available family and falls back to later entries when needed. End a stack with a generic family such as sans-serif, serif, or monospace. A named font may be unavailable, and missing glyphs can be rendered using fallback fonts too.
understand.whyItMatters: A resilient font stack avoids depending on one installed typeface. Test the writing systems used by learners because one font may not contain every script or symbol.
understand.analogy: A font stack is a list of preferred routes: if the first is unavailable, the next keeps the page readable.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy builds intuition; actual rendering follows CSS layout rules and browser specifications.

explain.narrative: The browser uses the first available font and falls back as needed. Replace the stack with Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif.

examples.explanation: The browser uses the first available font and falls back as needed. Replace the stack with Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered demonstration of the CSS behaviour described in this lesson.

practise.guidedTask: Create sans-serif, serif, and monospace examples. Explain why each stack ends with a generic family.
practise.independentTask: Why should a font-family stack end with a generic family?
hints: Change one declaration at a time and observe the result.
